strengths: Establishes a clear and non-trivial theoretical equivalence (Thm. 3.1/C.1) between the mean-field signal-propagation framework and the IGB framework for untrained networks, providing a unified view of initialization-induced predictive bias and trainability conditions

Yields an interesting and counter-intuitive insight (Prop. 4.1): the EOC/optimal trainability condition corresponds to 'transient deep prejudice' rather than neutrality, directly resolving an open question from prior IGB work [20]

Includes genuinely useful technical corrections and extensions: a proof that the correlation coefficient converges to 1 across the entire ReLU phase diagram (contradicting earlier claims in [4, 12]), clarification of order parameters for unbounded activations via χ̃1 (Lemma A.1, using Stein's lemma), and explicit IGB recursions for ReLU (App. G)

Extends the framework to non-zero bias variances and to multi-node activation functions (pooling layers), deriving general recursions and new EOC phase diagrams (Fig. 4) with practical implications for initialization design

The theory is validated empirically: simulations confirm the concentration/self-averaging behavior (Figs. 2, 5, 9), and initialization gradients on CIFAR10 confirm the vanishing/exploding gradient predictions (Fig. 7); reproducibility is aided by detailed recursive equations throughout the appendix
weaknesses: The central trainability claim (Prop. 4.1) is supported only by gradient-stability arguments at initialization; the paper provides no actual training experiments demonstrating that 'transient deep prejudice' initializations learn faster or better than neutral ones, leaving the headline 'bridging prejudice and trainability' claim under-validated in practice

Scope is narrow: analysis is confined to infinitely wide MLPs with i.i.d. standard Gaussian inputs, and the authors themselves show (App. D, Fig. 6) that both MF and IGB fail substantially for realistic finite widths (e.g., width 50), limiting immediate practical relevance to modern architectures

The i.i.d. Gaussian data assumption abstracts away real data structure; the fairness motivation raised in the introduction is only loosely connected to the actual results, which concern synthetic unstructured data and are unlikely to transfer directly to algorithmic fairness settings

Parts of the contribution are incremental relative to prior work: the equivalence is largely a consequence of the central limit theorem and the self-averaging results of [20], and the pooling-layer analysis is limited to n = 2 with mostly qualitative (shifted) phase diagrams

Presentation quality is uneven: numerous typos and grammatical issues (e.g., 'transient-deeep', 'resptc.', 'behwaviour', 'infinte-width'), and some proofs (e.g., Lemma B.3's reliance on self-averaging assumptions inherited from [20]) are brief and would benefit from more careful statements of regularity conditions

strengths: The paper makes a clean and correct-looking theoretical contribution: it formally proves the equivalence between the mean-field (MF) initialization framework and the initial guessing bias (IGB) framework in the infinite-width limit (Theorem 3.1), showing that the correlation coefficient c and the drift ratio γ are directly related (Eq. 8). This two-way mapping is a genuinely useful unification.

The derivation is carefully done, with proofs in the appendix (Stein's lemma applications, self-averaging arguments, Cauchy-Schwarz bounds) that appear sound, and the results are validated empirically: Fig. 2 shows good agreement between IGB predictions and MF confidence intervals, and Figs. 5 and 9 demonstrate convergence of finite-width experiments to the theoretical predictions.

The work identifies and corrects a substantive error in prior literature: the claim (Refs. [4], [12]) that the ReLU correlation coefficient fails to converge to 1 is disproven, with the explicit recursion in App. G deriving the correct convergence rates (exponential vs. power-law).

The extension of the MF/IGB analysis to multi-node activation functions (pooling layers) and to non-zero bias variances is a reasonable technical generalization, with a neat result (Lemma E.3) that MaxPool with symmetric activations leaves the EOC unchanged.
Writing is generally clear, and the paper is honest about limitations (confined to wide MLPs, infinite-width regime, failure of both theories for width-50 networks).
weaknesses: The headline claim — that optimal trainability requires a 'transient deep prejudice' rather than neutrality (Prop. 4.1) — is largely a repackaging of the standard EOC condition (χ̃1 = 1, c = 1) restated in IGB language. Once the equivalence of Theorem 3.1 is established, this 'counter-intuitive conclusion' follows almost immediately and its surprise value is overstated.

The evaluation is incomplete with respect to the paper's central claims. There are no training-dynamics experiments demonstrating that 'transient deep prejudice' initializations actually learn faster or better than neutral ones. The only real-data experiment is a gradient-magnitude measurement on CIFAR-10 (Fig. 7), which only illustrates the well-known vanishing/exploding gradient behavior. The practical significance of Prop. 4.1 is asserted, not demonstrated.

The fairness framing is overclaimed. The IGB analysis applies to i.i.d. Gaussian, unstructured data where class assignments are arbitrary; connecting this 'prejudice' to fairness concerns for real datasets (which the introduction invokes via [15–19]) is a rhetorical stretch that is never substantiated.

The analysis requires restrictive assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian inputs, infinite width, equal layer widths, identical weight/bias variances across layers). The paper itself shows (App. D, Fig. 6) that both theories fail for width-50 networks, which limits practical relevance; the discussion of the finite-width gap is superficial and deferred to future work.

Novelty is incremental. The paper builds heavily on the IGB framework of [20] and the MF machinery of [12] (even reusing their Algorithm 1 for the EOC). The main genuinely new ingredients are the equivalence theorem and the pooling extension, which together may be too narrow for a top-tier venue.

The pooling analysis is limited to n = 2 nodes and to observing a qualitative shift of phase boundaries in the (σ_b², σ_w²) plane; no practical initialization guidelines of demonstrable value emerge from this, despite the abstract promising them.

Numerous typos and rough edges ('transient-deeep', 'infinte-width', 'respct.', 'initializaton', Eq. numbering glitches, dangling Eq. 50), and the multi-node calculation in App. E contains a suspicious algebraic step (Eq. 51/52) whose justification should be checked more carefully; overall polish is below expectations.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper establishes a rigorous equivalence (Thm. 3.1/Thm. C.1) between the mean-field (MF) signal-propagation framework and the initial guessing bias (IGB) framework, unifying two previously separate lines of work on initialization.

The connection yields a genuinely interesting and non-obvious insight: the optimal trainability condition (EOC) corresponds to a state of 'transient deep prejudice' rather than neutrality, directly refuting the intuitive assumption in prior work [20]. This reframing of MF phases in terms of predictive bias is a new lens on initialization theory.

The theoretical development is careful and reasonably self-contained: the IGB framework is extended to non-zero bias terms (App. B), a corrected order parameter for unbounded activations is derived via Stein's lemma (App. A), and explicit recursions for ReLU are worked out in App. G, including the correction that the correlation coefficient always converges to one for ReLU (contradicting [4, 12]) — a concrete correction to the literature.

The multi-node extension (App. E) and the analysis of max/average pooling effects on phase diagrams (Fig. 4, Lemma E.3) is a practically relevant novelty, as pooling layers have received little attention in the MF literature.

The theory is empirically validated at multiple points: Fig. 2 (IGB predictions vs. MF confidence intervals), Fig. 5/9 (finite-width convergence of the theoretical predictions), and Fig. 7 (gradient vanishing/exploding behaviour across the phase transition).

The paper is honest about limitations: the infinite-width/Gaussian-data assumptions, the failure of both frameworks for finite networks (App. D), and the restriction to MLPs are all clearly acknowledged.
weaknesses: Scope is narrow: results are confined to wide MLPs with i.i.d. Gaussian inputs and (mostly) binary classification. It remains unclear how the MF-IGB correspondence, and the headline 'optimal initialization is biased' conclusion, carry over to convolutional/attention architectures or structured real-world data, which limits practical significance.

The main equivalence theorem is ultimately a consequence of the central limit theorem and self-averaging, so its technical depth is moderate; the paper's value rests more on the conceptual reinterpretation than on difficult mathematics.

The central trainability claim (Prop. 4.1) is largely inherited from classical EOC results [4, 12] combined with the new correspondence; there is no direct experimental evidence connecting initial prejudice states to downstream training speed or final accuracy on real tasks (e.g., learning curves as a function of initialization regime).

The fairness framing feels overstated: initial guessing bias on synthetic unstructured data is quite far from the sociotechnical fairness concerns cited [15-19], and the paper does not demonstrate any fairness-relevant consequence on real biased datasets.

Empirical validation is limited to synthetic Gaussian data and a single CIFAR10 gradient check (Fig. 7); no experiments with trained networks, multiple architectures, or non-Gaussian data distributions are provided.

Presentation issues: several typos and minor errors ('behviour', 'infinte-width', 'transiency', 'transient-deeep', 'respct.', 'initializaton', inconsistent lemma/theorem statements between main text and appendix, an unfinished numbering in Lemma E.1), which suggest the manuscript needed another careful proofreading pass.

strengths: The paper establishes a clean and rigorous equivalence (Thm. 3.1 / Thm. E.1) between the mean-field (MF) signal-propagation framework and the initial guessing bias (IGB) framework, including the explicit algebraic relation c = γ/(1+γ). The proofs (Stein's lemma derivations, explicit ReLU recursions in App. H) are careful and self-contained.

The central insight — that the edge-of-chaos / optimal-trainability initialization coincides with a state of 'transient deep prejudice' rather than neutrality — is counterintuitive, well-argued (Prop. 4.1), and directly addresses an open question raised in [20].

Concrete technical corrections to prior literature: the paper shows that for ReLU the correlation coefficient converges to c=1 across the whole phase diagram, contradicting claims in [4, 12], and derives the depth-scaling behavior of γ (exponential vs. power-law divergence) distinguishing ordered and chaotic deep prejudice.

The IGB framework is usefully generalized to non-zero bias variances and to multi-node activation functions (max/average pooling), with explicit EOC computations (e.g., EOC at σ_w² ≈ 1.10 for ReLU+MaxPool, ≈ 3.03 for ReLU+AvgPool).

Empirical validation spans multiple architectures (MLP, residual MLP, vanilla ViT, and a ~300M pre-trained ViT fine-tuned on CIFAR100), with consistent qualitative agreement between theoretical phase boundaries and observed training dynamics, and honest discussion of limitations (infinite-width/infinite-data regime, no feature learning).
weaknesses: The theory is restricted to i.i.d. standard Gaussian inputs in the infinite-width-then-infinite-data limit, which is far from realistic image/text data. The paper acknowledges this, but it substantially weakens the practical significance of the 'bias helps learning' claim; the largest ViT experiment requires artificially rescaling all pre-trained weights by σ_w² to 'trigger' phase behavior, which is a fairly loose and somewhat engineered connection to the theory.

The equivalence result itself is arguably incremental: once the data average is taken at fixed weights, the identity q_ab = σ²_μ and the relation c = γ/(1+γ) follow fairly directly; a knowledgeable reader may find the main theorem unsurprising, with the novelty residing mostly in reinterpretation and extensions.

Training experiments lack baselines and breadth: few optimizers/hyperparameter settings (Adam only, single lr per configuration, unclear number of seeds), and conclusions such as 'neutrality performs poorly' or 'ordered phase eventually matches EOC' rest on limited configurations with post-hoc explanations (e.g., Adam momentum effects) rather than controlled evidence.

The fairness framing in the introduction and abstract (connecting IGB to societal bias concerns [15–19]) is overstated — the theory concerns random Gaussian data at initialization and has little direct bearing on algorithmic fairness in trained models on structured data.

Some technical claims rely on approximations that are stated informally (e.g., gradient recursion Eq. (90)-(91) assuming forward/backward independence, informal Lemma D.3 with a broken equation reference 'Eq. (??)'), and several typos/notation slips ('behviour', 'posseses', 'infinte-width', W((l))) reduce polish.

Only ReLU/Tanh (and GeLU in the ViT) are treated in depth; the breadth of activation functions for which the full phase taxonomy is validated empirically is narrow, and the multi-class IGB analysis is largely relegated to the binary case.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and interesting question: connecting the initial guessing bias (IGB) framework with mean-field (MF) theories of initialization, and the resulting reinterpretation of the edge of chaos as a maximally biased state is a non-obvious and somewhat counterintuitive insight.

The theoretical development is substantive: the equivalence theorem (Thm. 3.1 / E.1) relating drift ratio gamma to the correlation coefficient c, the corrected order parameter chi-tilde_1 for unbounded activations, and the detailed ReLU analysis (App. H) are worked out carefully, with extensive supplementary derivations.

The empirical validation is reasonably broad in scope, covering MLPs, residual MLPs, vanilla ViTs, and a large pre-trained ViT (~300M parameters), across binarized and multi-class datasets, and the paper extends the IGB framework to non-zero biases and pooling layers.

The paper corrects an apparent inaccuracy in prior MF phase diagrams for ReLU (the correlation coefficient converging to one across the whole phase diagram), which is a useful contribution to the initialization literature.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is a fairly direct variance decomposition: q_aa = sigma^2_mu + sigma^2_y and c = gamma/(1+gamma) follow almost immediately from the Gaussian assumptions. The 'equivalence' is more a change of variables than a deep theorem, and the main insight (EOC implies biased initialization) essentially follows by definition of c = 1. The novelty over [4, 12, 20] feels incremental.

The theory rests on the restrictive assumption that the dataset consists of i.i.d. standard Gaussian samples. This is far from any realistic data distribution, and the paper provides no analysis or even discussion of how structured, class-imbalanced, or correlated real data would modify the IGB/MG mapping. The claimed relevance to fairness is therefore largely rhetorical.

All results are confined to the infinite-width, infinite-data limit, which the authors themselves acknowledge does not exhibit feature learning. The bridge from this regime to the practical training experiments is only asserted, not established — finite-width corrections are precisely where the theory is weakest, and the agreement shown in Fig. 2 is for a single very wide (N=10,000) configuration.

The training experiments do not cleanly support the headline claim. On BFMNIST the ordered-deep-prejudice phase eventually reaches similar performance to the EOC (with an unexplained 'sudden performance jump'), and the MLP on CIFAR10 plateaus near 50% accuracy, undermining the notion that EOC is distinctly optimal. The dependence on Adam and momentum effects is acknowledged but not analyzed.

The large ViT experiment is artificial: phase behavior is induced by manually rescaling all pre-trained weights by arbitrary factors (sigma_w^2 in {0.5, 1, 1.5}), which degrades the pre-trained solution and says little about natural initialization regimes.

Several rigor and clarity issues: broken equation references (Eq. (??)), an unnumbered/incorrectly referenced figure in Lemma F.7's proof, a duplicated row in Table 2, and scattered typos ('behviour', 'transiency', 'posseses', 'tranformer'). Key propositions (e.g., Prop. 4.1) are essentially restatements of the equivalence rather than independently proven claims.

The scope is essentially limited to unnormalized MLPs and ViTs with norms removed; batch/layer normalization, skip connections, and other standard components are explicitly excluded, which further limits the practical significance of the 'transient deep prejudice' conclusion for modern architectures.

Given the significant prior literature on MF initialization ([4], [12], [14]) and on IGB ([20], [24]), the paper's positioning as a bridging work is reasonable, but the marginal gain over reading both frameworks side-by-side is not compelling enough for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper establishes a clean and formally proven equivalence (Thm. 3.1 / Thm. E.1) between the mean-field (MF) signal-propagation framework and the initial guessing bias (IGB) framework, mapping q(l)aa ↔ σ²μ+σ²y, q(l)ab ↔ σ²μ, and c(l)ab = γ(l)/(1+γ(l)). This unification is a genuine conceptual contribution that connects two previously separate lines of work (Schoenholz et al./Hayou et al. vs. Francazi et al.).

The characterization of ReLU networks' correlation coefficient converging to c=1 across the entire phase diagram (Lemma C.2, Lemma H.1) corrects inaccuracies in prior MF phase-diagram analyses, and the detailed phase taxonomy (ordered/transient/chaotic deep prejudice, prejudice, neutrality, Tab. 1) provides a finer structure than prior work.

The central claim (Prop. 4.1) that optimal trainability coincides with a transient deep-prejudice state is counterintuitive and directly answers an open question from [20]; the theoretical argument is backed by gradient-stability reasoning and training experiments across MLPs, residual MLPs, vanilla ViTs, and a fine-tuned 300M-parameter ViT.

The extension of IGB to non-zero bias terms (App. D) and to multi-node activation functions such as max/average pooling (App. F) broadens applicability, and the appendices contain substantial, mostly careful derivations (Stein's lemma usage, exact recursions for ReLU, closed-form I(γ)).

Empirical validation is reasonable in breadth: theory–experiment agreement for c(l)ab, γ(l), q(l)aa, q(l)ab with growing width (Figs. 2, 14–18, 27), plus training dynamics across the phases consistent with the propositions.
weaknesses: The theoretical framework is confined to the strict infinite-width-then-infinite-data mean-field regime, where no feature learning occurs; the authors acknowledge this, but it limits the practical relevance of the 'optimal initialization is biased' message to modern feature-learning regimes (proportional limit, NTK vs. lazy training) that are left unexplored.

The main equivalence result is essentially an observation that the two frameworks average the same quantities in different orders, rather than a deep structural result; parts of the machinery (EOC, gradient recursions) closely follow Hayou et al. [12], so the novelty is meaningful but incremental from a technical standpoint.

Training experiments are relatively weak support for Prop. 4.1: only a handful of phase settings per architecture, no error bars/seeds reported for the training curves, no comparison against more standard initialization schemes (e.g., He/Kaiming or edge-of-chaos variants with normalization), and the learning rates in Tab. 2 (e.g., 1e-7) appear unusually small and are not justified; the conclusion that the ordered phase 'eventually matches EOC' is attributed to optimizer effects without analysis.

The fairness framing in the introduction is loosely connected to the actual contribution: the theory assumes i.i.d. Gaussian inputs and concerns class imbalance for unstructured data, whereas real fairness concerns involve structured, correlated data; the paper does not demonstrate any consequence for fairness-relevant settings, so the broader claims overstate the scope.

Presentation issues remain: several typos and broken references ('transiency-deeep prejudice', Eq. (??) in Lemma D.3, Fig. ??, 'it is immediate to verify', 'behviour'), and some proofs are informal or sketchy (Thm. D.2 proof reduces to extending a Gaussianity argument; the V-operator symmetry argument in Lemma F.3 assumes conditions whose necessity is not clearly motivated).
